**SIL Global** (formerly known as the **Summer Institute of Linguistics International**) is an evangelical Christian nonprofit organization whose main purpose is to study, develop and document languages, especially those that are lesser-known, to expand linguistic knowledge, promote literacy, translate the Christian Bible into local languages, and aid minority language development.
Based on its language documentation work, SIL publishes a database, _Ethnologue_, of its research into the world's languages, and develops and publishes software programs for language documentation, such as FieldWorks Language Explorer (FLEx)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Fi-2) and Lexique Pro.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Lexique_Pro-3)
Its main offices in the United States are located at the International Linguistics Center in Dallas, Texas.

William Cameron Townsend, a Presbyterian minister, founded the organization in 1934, after undertaking a Christian mission with the Disciples of Christ among the Kaqchikel Maya people in Guatemala in the early 1930s.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-G255-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-5) In 1933, he turned to Mexico to translate the Bible into indigenous languages there, as he had done for Kaqchikel. Townsend established a working relationship with the Mexican Secretariat of Public Education under the government of President Lázaro Cárdenas (in office 1934–1940) and founded SIL to educate linguist-missionaries to work in Mexico. Because the Mexican government did not allow missionary work through its educational system, Townsend founded Wycliffe Bible Translators in 1942 as a separate organization from SIL. Wycliffe Bible Translators focused on Bible translation and missionary activities, whereas SIL focused on linguistic documentation and literacy education.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-6)
Having initiated collaboration with the Mexican education authorities, Townsend started the institute as a small summer training session in Sulphur Springs, Arkansas, in 1934 to train missionaries in basic linguistic, anthropological, and translation principles. Through the following decades, the SIL linguists worked at providing literacy education to indigenous people of Mexico, while simultaneously working with the Wycliffe Bible Translators on Bible translation. One of the students at the first summer institute in its second year, 1935, Kenneth Lee Pike (1912–2000), would become the foremost figure in the history of SIL.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-G255-4) He served as SIL's president from 1942 to 1979, then as president emeritus until he died in 2000.

### Instituto Lingüístico de Verano
[edit]
The Mexican branch, _Instituto Lingüístico de Verano_, was established in 1948.

### Kidnapping and murder of Chester A. Bitterman in Colombia
[edit]
On January 19, 1981, SIL field worker Chester "Chet" A. Bitterman was taken hostage by far-left guerilla group M-19 in Colombia who believed SIL was a cover operation for the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA). SIL denied involvement with any government intelligence agency stating that it was against their policy.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-8)
M-19 demanded SIL withdraw all 209 of its people from Colombia, or else they would kill Bitterman. After 48 days of SIL refusing to yield to the demands, Bitterman was found murdered.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-9)
In 2016, Michel Kenmogne from Cameroon became executive director. In 2025, Johnstone Ndunde became executive director.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-10)
In 2023, SIL said it had 1,350 language projects in 98 countries and 4,200 staff from 84 countries.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:0-11) By 2023, this had risen to 1,530 language projects in 107 countries, with a corresponding increase in staff to 4,373 people from 86 countries.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:0-11) The organization reports that these languages are spoken by 950 million people.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-12)
The vision of SIL Global is: "We long to see people flourishing in community using the languages they value most." Their mission states: "Inspired by God's love, we advocate, build capacity, and work with local communities to apply language expertise that advances meaningful development, education, and engagement with Scripture."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:0-11)

### Kidnapping and murder of Chester A. Bitterman in Colombia
SIL's principal contribution to linguistics has been the data that have been gathered and analyzed from over 1,000 minority and endangered languages,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-13) many of which had not been previously studied academically. SIL endeavors to share both its data and the results of its analysis to contribute to the overall knowledge of language. This has resulted in publications on languages such as Hixkaryana and Pirahã, which have challenged the universality of some linguistic theories. SIL's work has resulted in over 20,000 technical publications, all of which are listed in the SIL Bibliography.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-14) Most of these are a reflection of linguistic fieldwork.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-15)
SIL's focus has not been on the development of new linguistic theories, but tagmemics, though no longer promoted by SIL, was developed by Kenneth Pike, who also coined the words emic and etic, more widely used today in anthropology.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-16)
Another focus of SIL is literacy work, particularly in indigenous languages. SIL assists local, regional, and national agencies that are developing formal and informal education in vernacular languages. These cooperative efforts enable new advances in the complex field of educational development in multilingual and multicultural societies.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-17)
SIL provides instructors and instructional materials for linguistics programs at several major institutions of higher learning around the world. In the United States, these include Dallas International University, Biola University, Moody Bible Institute, and Dallas Theological Seminary. Other universities with SIL programs include Trinity Western University in Canada, Charles Darwin University in Australia, and Universidad Ricardo Palma in Lima, Peru.
The organization has recently established a new Language and Culture Documentation Services Unit that aims to preserve and revitalize languages threatened by extinction. The creation of this department reflects a growing interest in documenting endangered languages and incorporates a multidisciplinary approach to anthropology and linguistics.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-La-18)

### Kidnapping and murder of Chester A. Bitterman in Colombia
SIL has Consultative Status with UNESCO as an NGO and has Special Consultative Status with the United Nations Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC) as an advocate for ethnolinguistic communities.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-19)
The organization is a member of the Forum of Bible Agencies International and Micah Network, and is a founding member of Maaya, the World Network for Linguistic Diversity.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-20)

**SIL Global** (formerly known as the **Summer Institute of Linguistics International**) is an evangelical Christian nonprofit organization whose main purpose is to study, develop and document languages, especially those that are lesser-known, to expand linguistic knowledge, promote literacy, translate the Christian Bible into local languages, and aid minority language development.
Based on its language documentation work, SIL publishes a database, _Ethnologue_, of its research into the world's languages, and develops and publishes software programs for language documentation, such as FieldWorks Language Explorer (FLEx)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Fi-2) and Lexique Pro.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Lexique_Pro-3)
Its main offices in the United States are located at the International Linguistics Center in Dallas, Texas.
texts.1:
William Cameron Townsend, a Presbyterian minister, founded the organization in 1934, after undertaking a Christian mission with the Disciples of Christ among the Kaqchikel Maya people in Guatemala in the early 1930s.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-G255-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-5) In 1933, he turned to Mexico to translate the Bible into indigenous languages there, as he had done for Kaqchikel. Townsend established a working relationship with the Mexican Secretariat of Public Education under the government of President Lázaro Cárdenas (in office 1934–1940) and founded SIL to educate linguist-missionaries to work in Mexico. Because the Mexican government did not allow missionary work through its educational system, Townsend founded Wycliffe Bible Translators in 1942 as a separate organization from SIL. Wycliffe Bible Translators focused on Bible translation and missionary activities, whereas SIL focused on linguistic documentation and literacy education.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-6)
Having initiated collaboration with the Mexican education authorities, Townsend started the institute as a small summer training session in Sulphur Springs, Arkansas, in 1934 to train missionaries in basic linguistic, anthropological, and translation principles. Through the following decades, the SIL linguists worked at providing literacy education to indigenous people of Mexico, while simultaneously working with the Wycliffe Bible Translators on Bible translation. One of the students at the first summer institute in its second year, 1935, Kenneth Lee Pike (1912–2000), would become the foremost figure in the history of SIL.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-G255-4) He served as SIL's president from 1942 to 1979, then as president emeritus until he died in 2000.

**SIL Global** (formerly known as the **Summer Institute of Linguistics International**) is an evangelical Christian nonprofit organization whose main purpose is to study, develop and document languages, especially those that are lesser-known, to expand linguistic knowledge, promote literacy, translate the Christian Bible into local languages, and aid minority language development.
Based on its language documentation work, SIL publishes a database, _Ethnologue_, of its research into the world's languages, and develops and publishes software programs for language documentation, such as FieldWorks Language Explorer (FLEx)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Fi-2) and Lexique Pro.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Lexique_Pro-3)
Its main offices in the United States are located at the International Linguistics Center in Dallas, Texas.

William Cameron Townsend, a Presbyterian minister, founded the organization in 1934, after undertaking a Christian mission with the Disciples of Christ among the Kaqchikel Maya people in Guatemala in the early 1930s.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-G255-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-5) In 1933, he turned to Mexico to translate the Bible into indigenous languages there, as he had done for Kaqchikel. Townsend established a working relationship with the Mexican Secretariat of Public Education under the government of President Lázaro Cárdenas (in office 1934–1940) and founded SIL to educate linguist-missionaries to work in Mexico. Because the Mexican government did not allow missionary work through its educational system, Townsend founded Wycliffe Bible Translators in 1942 as a separate organization from SIL. Wycliffe Bible Translators focused on Bible translation and missionary activities, whereas SIL focused on linguistic documentation and literacy education.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-6)
Having initiated collaboration with the Mexican education authorities, Townsend started the institute as a small summer training session in Sulphur Springs, Arkansas, in 1934 to train missionaries in basic linguistic, anthropological, and translation principles. Through the following decades, the SIL linguists worked at providing literacy education to indigenous people of Mexico, while simultaneously working with the Wycliffe Bible Translators on Bible translation. One of the students at the first summer institute in its second year, 1935, Kenneth Lee Pike (1912–2000), would become the foremost figure in the history of SIL.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-G255-4) He served as SIL's president from 1942 to 1979, then as president emeritus until he died in 2000.

### Instituto Lingüístico de Verano
[edit]
The Mexican branch, _Instituto Lingüístico de Verano_, was established in 1948.

### Kidnapping and murder of Chester A. Bitterman in Colombia
[edit]
On January 19, 1981, SIL field worker Chester "Chet" A. Bitterman was taken hostage by far-left guerilla group M-19 in Colombia who believed SIL was a cover operation for the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA). SIL denied involvement with any government intelligence agency stating that it was against their policy.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-8)
M-19 demanded SIL withdraw all 209 of its people from Colombia, or else they would kill Bitterman. After 48 days of SIL refusing to yield to the demands, Bitterman was found murdered.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-9)
In 2016, Michel Kenmogne from Cameroon became executive director. In 2025, Johnstone Ndunde became executive director.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-10)
In 2023, SIL said it had 1,350 language projects in 98 countries and 4,200 staff from 84 countries.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:0-11) By 2023, this had risen to 1,530 language projects in 107 countries, with a corresponding increase in staff to 4,373 people from 86 countries.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:0-11) The organization reports that these languages are spoken by 950 million people.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-12)
The vision of SIL Global is: "We long to see people flourishing in community using the languages they value most." Their mission states: "Inspired by God's love, we advocate, build capacity, and work with local communities to apply language expertise that advances meaningful development, education, and engagement with Scripture."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:0-11)

### Kidnapping and murder of Chester A. Bitterman in Colombia
SIL's principal contribution to linguistics has been the data that have been gathered and analyzed from over 1,000 minority and endangered languages,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-13) many of which had not been previously studied academically. SIL endeavors to share both its data and the results of its analysis to contribute to the overall knowledge of language. This has resulted in publications on languages such as Hixkaryana and Pirahã, which have challenged the universality of some linguistic theories. SIL's work has resulted in over 20,000 technical publications, all of which are listed in the SIL Bibliography.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-14) Most of these are a reflection of linguistic fieldwork.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-15)
SIL's focus has not been on the development of new linguistic theories, but tagmemics, though no longer promoted by SIL, was developed by Kenneth Pike, who also coined the words emic and etic, more widely used today in anthropology.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-16)
Another focus of SIL is literacy work, particularly in indigenous languages. SIL assists local, regional, and national agencies that are developing formal and informal education in vernacular languages. These cooperative efforts enable new advances in the complex field of educational development in multilingual and multicultural societies.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-17)
SIL provides instructors and instructional materials for linguistics programs at several major institutions of higher learning around the world. In the United States, these include Dallas International University, Biola University, Moody Bible Institute, and Dallas Theological Seminary. Other universities with SIL programs include Trinity Western University in Canada, Charles Darwin University in Australia, and Universidad Ricardo Palma in Lima, Peru.
The organization has recently established a new Language and Culture Documentation Services Unit that aims to preserve and revitalize languages threatened by extinction. The creation of this department reflects a growing interest in documenting endangered languages and incorporates a multidisciplinary approach to anthropology and linguistics.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-La-18)

SIL has Consultative Status with UNESCO as an NGO and has Special Consultative Status with the United Nations Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC) as an advocate for ethnolinguistic communities.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-19)
The organization is a member of the Forum of Bible Agencies International and Micah Network, and is a founding member of Maaya, the World Network for Linguistic Diversity.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-20)

## Summary
We are a global, faith-based nonprofit that works with local communities around the world to develop language solutions that expand possibilities for a better life. SIL's core contribution areas are Bible translation, literacy, education, development, linguistic research and language tools.
We are eager for the day when all people enjoy equal access to education, to socio-economic opportunities, and to resources for spiritual growth - no matter what language they speak or sign.

## Purpose
We long to see people flourishing in community using the languages they value most.
SIL's service with ethnolinguistic minority communities is motivated by the belief that all people are created in the image of God, and that languages and cultures are part of the richness of God's creation. SIL is founded on the principle that communities should be able to pursue their social, cultural, political, economic and spiritual goals without sacrificing their ethnolinguistic identity. As a faith-based nonprofit organization, SIL works alongside language communities as they discover how to harness the power of their language to address challenges and reach their goals.

## Mission statement
Inspired by God's love, we advocate, build capacity, and work with local communities to apply language expertise that advances meaningful development, education, and engagement with Scripture.

## History
The principal founder of SIL International was William Cameron Townsend (1896-1982). He began cross-cultural work with the Kaqchikel people of Guatemala in 1919. By 1929, Townsend's vision had broadened to include other peoples who also needed language development. SIL International (then known as the Summer Institute of Linguistics) began in 1934 as a summer training program in Arkansas, USA, with two students. The enrollment of these summer classes grew each subsequent year.
Kenneth L. Pike (1912-2000) was one of five students in the 1935 course. He began work on the Mixtec language in the state of Oaxaca, Mexico. This work launched Pike into his life-long work in linguistics and the study of language in the context of human behavior. Dr. Pike served as President of SIL until 1979.
For a timeline, visit: sil.org/about/history
* * *

## Program accomplishments
As of October 2021, we are involved in approximately 1,633 active language projects in 98 countries. These projects impact more than 855+ million people within 1,347 local communities. SIL's work brings together more than 4,200 staff from 84 countries who work alongside thousands more local partners and community volunteers worldwide.

Board chair Hans Combrink[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Leaders-1)  
AffiliationsEvangelical Christianity

Formerly called Summer Institute of Linguistics
**SIL Global** (formerly known as the **Summer Institute of Linguistics International**) is an evangelical Christian nonprofit organization whose main purpose is to study, develop and document languages, especially those that are lesser-known, to expand linguistic knowledge, promote literacy, translate the Christian Bible into local languages, and aid minority language development.
Based on its language documentation work, SIL publishes a database, _Ethnologue_, of its research into the world's languages, and develops and publishes software programs for language documentation, such as FieldWorks Language Explorer (FLEx)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Fi-2) and Lexique Pro.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Lexique_Pro-3)
Its main offices in the United States are located at the International Linguistics Center in Dallas, Texas.

William Cameron Townsend, a Presbyterian minister, founded the organization in 1934, after undertaking a Christian mission with the Disciples of Christ among the Kaqchikel Maya people in Guatemala in the early 1930s.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-G255-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-5) In 1933, he turned to Mexico to translate the Bible into indigenous languages there, as he had done for Kaqchikel. Townsend established a working relationship with the Mexican Secretariat of Public Education under the government of President Lázaro Cárdenas (in office 1934–1940) and founded SIL to educate linguist-missionaries to work in Mexico. Because the Mexican government did not allow missionary work through its educational system, Townsend founded Wycliffe Bible Translators in 1942 as a separate organization from SIL. Wycliffe Bible Translators focused on Bible translation and missionary activities, whereas SIL focused on linguistic documentation and literacy education.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-6)
Having initiated collaboration with the Mexican education authorities, Townsend started the institute as a small summer training session in Sulphur Springs, Arkansas, in 1934 to train missionaries in basic linguistic, anthropological, and translation principles. Through the following decades, the SIL linguists worked at providing literacy education to indigenous people of Mexico, while simultaneously working with the Wycliffe Bible Translators on Bible translation. One of the students at the first summer institute in its second year, 1935, Kenneth Lee Pike (1912–2000), would become the foremost figure in the history of SIL.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-G255-4) He served as SIL's president from 1942 to 1979, then as president emeritus until he died in 2000.

### Instituto Lingüístico de Verano
[edit]
The Mexican branch, _Instituto Lingüístico de Verano_, was established in 1948.

### Kidnapping and murder of Chester A. Bitterman in Colombia
[edit]
On January 19, 1981, SIL field worker Chester "Chet" A. Bitterman was taken hostage by far-left guerilla group M-19 in Colombia who believed SIL was a cover operation for the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA). SIL denied involvement with any government intelligence agency stating that it was against their policy.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-8)
M-19 demanded SIL withdraw all 209 of its people from Colombia, or else they would kill Bitterman. After 48 days of SIL refusing to yield to the demands, Bitterman was found murdered.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-9)
In 2016, Michel Kenmogne from Cameroon became executive director. In 2025, Johnstone Ndunde became executive director.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-10)
In 2023, SIL said it had 1,350 language projects in 98 countries and 4,200 staff from 84 countries.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:0-11) By 2023, this had risen to 1,530 language projects in 107 countries, with a corresponding increase in staff to 4,373 people from 86 countries.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:0-11) The organization reports that these languages are spoken by 950 million people.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-12)
The vision of SIL Global is: "We long to see people flourishing in community using the languages they value most." Their mission states: "Inspired by God's love, we advocate, build capacity, and work with local communities to apply language expertise that advances meaningful development, education, and engagement with Scripture."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:0-11)

### Kidnapping and murder of Chester A. Bitterman in Colombia
SIL's principal contribution to linguistics has been the data that have been gathered and analyzed from over 1,000 minority and endangered languages,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-13) many of which had not been previously studied academically. SIL endeavors to share both its data and the results of its analysis to contribute to the overall knowledge of language. This has resulted in publications on languages such as Hixkaryana and Pirahã, which have challenged the universality of some linguistic theories. SIL's work has resulted in over 20,000 technical publications, all of which are listed in the SIL Bibliography.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-14) Most of these are a reflection of linguistic fieldwork.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-15)
SIL's focus has not been on the development of new linguistic theories, but tagmemics, though no longer promoted by SIL, was developed by Kenneth Pike, who also coined the words emic and etic, more widely used today in anthropology.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-16)
Another focus of SIL is literacy work, particularly in indigenous languages. SIL assists local, regional, and national agencies that are developing formal and informal education in vernacular languages. These cooperative efforts enable new advances in the complex field of educational development in multilingual and multicultural societies.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-17)
SIL provides instructors and instructional materials for linguistics programs at several major institutions of higher learning around the world. In the United States, these include Dallas International University, Biola University, Moody Bible Institute, and Dallas Theological Seminary. Other universities with SIL programs include Trinity Western University in Canada, Charles Darwin University in Australia, and Universidad Ricardo Palma in Lima, Peru.
The organization has recently established a new Language and Culture Documentation Services Unit that aims to preserve and revitalize languages threatened by extinction. The creation of this department reflects a growing interest in documenting endangered languages and incorporates a multidisciplinary approach to anthropology and linguistics.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-La-18)

### Kidnapping and murder of Chester A. Bitterman in Colombia
SIL has Consultative Status with UNESCO as an NGO and has Special Consultative Status with the United Nations Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC) as an advocate for ethnolinguistic communities.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-19)
The organization is a member of the Forum of Bible Agencies International and Micah Network, and is a founding member of Maaya, the World Network for Linguistic Diversity.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-20)

## Summary
We are a global, faith-based nonprofit that works with local communities around the world to develop language solutions that expand possibilities for a better life. SIL's core contribution areas are Bible translation, literacy, education, development, linguistic research and language tools.
We are eager for the day when all people enjoy equal access to education, to socio-economic opportunities, and to resources for spiritual growth - no matter what language they speak or sign.

## Purpose
We long to see people flourishing in community using the languages they value most.
SIL's service with ethnolinguistic minority communities is motivated by the belief that all people are created in the image of God, and that languages and cultures are part of the richness of God's creation. SIL is founded on the principle that communities should be able to pursue their social, cultural, political, economic and spiritual goals without sacrificing their ethnolinguistic identity. As a faith-based nonprofit organization, SIL works alongside language communities as they discover how to harness the power of their language to address challenges and reach their goals.

texts.20:
## History
The principal founder of SIL International was William Cameron Townsend (1896-1982). He began cross-cultural work with the Kaqchikel people of Guatemala in 1919. By 1929, Townsend's vision had broadened to include other peoples who also needed language development. SIL International (then known as the Summer Institute of Linguistics) began in 1934 as a summer training program in Arkansas, USA, with two students. The enrollment of these summer classes grew each subsequent year.
Kenneth L. Pike (1912-2000) was one of five students in the 1935 course. He began work on the Mixtec language in the state of Oaxaca, Mexico. This work launched Pike into his life-long work in linguistics and the study of language in the context of human behavior. Dr. Pike served as President of SIL until 1979.
For a timeline, visit: sil.org/about/history

**SIL Global** (formerly known as the **Summer Institute of Linguistics International**) is an evangelical Christian nonprofit organization whose main purpose is to study, develop and document languages, especially those that are lesser-known, to expand linguistic knowledge, promote literacy, translate the Christian Bible into local languages, and aid minority language development.
Based on its language documentation work, SIL publishes a database, _Ethnologue_, of its research into the world's languages, and develops and publishes software programs for language documentation, such as FieldWorks Language Explorer (FLEx)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Fi-2) and Lexique Pro.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Lexique_Pro-3)
Its main offices in the United States are located at the International Linguistics Center in Dallas, Texas.

William Cameron Townsend, a Presbyterian minister, founded the organization in 1934, after undertaking a Christian mission with the Disciples of Christ among the Kaqchikel Maya people in Guatemala in the early 1930s.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-G255-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-5) In 1933, he turned to Mexico to translate the Bible into indigenous languages there, as he had done for Kaqchikel. Townsend established a working relationship with the Mexican Secretariat of Public Education under the government of President Lázaro Cárdenas (in office 1934–1940) and founded SIL to educate linguist-missionaries to work in Mexico. Because the Mexican government did not allow missionary work through its educational system, Townsend founded Wycliffe Bible Translators in 1942 as a separate organization from SIL. Wycliffe Bible Translators focused on Bible translation and missionary activities, whereas SIL focused on linguistic documentation and literacy education.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-6)
Having initiated collaboration with the Mexican education authorities, Townsend started the institute as a small summer training session in Sulphur Springs, Arkansas, in 1934 to train missionaries in basic linguistic, anthropological, and translation principles. Through the following decades, the SIL linguists worked at providing literacy education to indigenous people of Mexico, while simultaneously working with the Wycliffe Bible Translators on Bible translation. One of the students at the first summer institute in its second year, 1935, Kenneth Lee Pike (1912–2000), would become the foremost figure in the history of SIL.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-G255-4) He served as SIL's president from 1942 to 1979, then as president emeritus until he died in 2000.

Bitterman was taken hostage by far-left guerilla group M-19 in Colombia who believed SIL was a cover operation for the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA). SIL endeavors to share both its data and the results of its analysis to contribute to the overall knowledge of language. This has resulted in publications on languages such as Hixkaryana and Pirahã, which have challenged the universality of some linguistic theories. SIL's work has resulted in over 20,000 technical publications, all of which are listed in the SIL Bibliography.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-14) Most of these are a reflection of linguistic fieldwork.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-15)
SIL's focus has not been on the development of new linguistic theories, but tagmemics, though no longer promoted by SIL, was developed by Kenneth Pike, who also coined the words emic and etic, more widely used today in anthropology.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-16)
Another focus of SIL is literacy work, particularly in indigenous languages. SIL assists local, regional, and national agencies that are developing formal and informal education in vernacular languages. These cooperative efforts enable new advances in the complex field of educational development in multilingual and multicultural societies.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-17)
SIL provides instructors and instructional materials for linguistics programs at several major institutions of higher learning around the world. The organization has recently established a new Language and Culture Documentation Services Unit that aims to preserve and revitalize languages threatened by extinction. The creation of this department reflects a growing interest in documenting endangered languages and incorporates a multidisciplinary approach to anthropology and linguistics.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-La-18)

The final step before automatic translation starts involves creation of a viable starter training and test data set for training the multilingual model of Flores-200This is referred to as ‘seed data’ and described as “a set of professionally-translated sentences in the Wikipedia domain” (NLLB Team et al. 2022: 23). Due to being human produced and thus less likely to contain hallucinations (Förster and Skop, this volume), it is presented as vital for ensuring high-quality translation outputs. The development of ‘seed data’ follows the same overall procedure as that used to create the ‘benchmark’ data set, see Fig.1, but “consists of translations from 842 distinct web articles, totaling 3001 sentences” (NLLB Team et al. 2022: 22). These sentences are assembled using an intricate process presumably to ensure some elusive notion of representativeness. The process is described as follows:
> Data for NLLB-Seed was sampled from Wikimedia’s _List of articles every Wikipedia should have_, a collection of 10,000 Wikidata IDs corresponding to notable topics in different fields of knowledge and human activity. These are split into 11 categories such as _People, History, Philosophy and Religion, Geography_. We uniformly sampled a subset of IDs from which we would draw data, and mapped these to the corresponding English Wikipedia articles. From each of these articles we then sampled the data that would be sent to translators. Instead of extracting individual sentences, which would have left translators with little context to work with, we chose to sample triplets of contiguous sentences, ensuring no more than one triplet per article was used (similar to Flores-200). (NLLB Team et al. 2022: 23-24).

## 4 Language making for machine learning technologies
The resulting human translations are checked by automatic processes (cf Kreutzer et al. [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-025-02389-5#ref-CR30 "Kreutzer J et al. (2021) Quality at a glance: an audit of web-crawled multilingual datasets. Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics,   
                  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2103.12028.pdf
.")) before they are used for training. Although this process is hailed as groundbreaking (NLLB Team et al. 2022: 23), persistent challenges such as mistranslations and other kinds of hallucinations remain.
The selection of languages for such artificial data creation is presented as a principle-based process. For example, to obtain a list of 200 languages, NLLB Team et al. (2022: 12) initially created “a preliminary list of over 250 possible language candidates”, and then whittled it down to 200 languages as follows:
> First, we considered all languages with a Wikipedia presence. [...] Wikipedia is a key site of knowledge dissemination for many speaking low-resource languages [...]  
>   
>   
> Next, we solicited lists of languages spoken in various regions by native speakers, focusing particularly on African languages—a category of languages that have historically been underrepresented in translation efforts (Nekoto et al., 2020).  
>   
>   
> We then examined language coverage in multiple existing datasets in the natural language processing community, paying focused attention on training datasets without accompanying evaluation datasets.  
>   
>   
> Finally, we considered the adoption and usage of each language by looking at the approximate number of native speakers and other community-level variables relevant to our work.  
>   
>   
> Next, for each of the language candidates, we partnered with linguists from various specialized language service providers to understand if each of these languages has a standardized written form [...] because having a reliable, high-quality evaluation dataset is critical to accelerated experimental progress (NLLB Team et al. 2022: 12, 16).

## 4 Language making for machine learning technologies
This procedure illustrates the ‘opportunity of optimization’ approach that drives commercial entities’ engagement: the selection of languages is guided by easy and cheap access to data and the potential to reap monetary profits rather than the much cited concerns for improving the lives of disenfranchised people. This is also openly admitted when they state that: “deciding which languages to include in the final list ultimately came down to assessing the potential impact we might have on the respective low-resource language communities” (NLLB Team et al. 2022: 17) and “many of the languages that made the final cut have a presence on Wikipedia” (NLLB Team et al. 2022: 17). By contrast, languages with low speaker numbers that lack “written standards or [that] are predominantly oral” (NLLB Team et al. 2022: 17), whose cosmologies do not easily fit with the western symbolic order, or, interestingly, for whom the team could not identify clear needs for machine translation (for unspecified reasons) or sensed potential (undefined) risks were excluded.

## 4 Language making for machine learning technologies
Once identified for inclusion, languages are also categorized for easy digital access further fashioning them into discrete tangible artifacts, and ensuring alignment with existing language regimes in the Global North. NLLB, for instance, classifies each language in Flores-200 by recording its web support such as whether it is supported by Google Translate and Microsoft Translate, its resource level, i.e., “if there are fewer than 1 M publicly available, de-duplicated bitext samples with any other language within our set of 200 languages” (NLLB Team et al. 2022: 17) and by assigning it an ISO 639–3 code, a ISO 15924 script subtag, and a unique name, which is necessary “due to formatting limitations” even though a language might locally be identified by multiple names. Interestingly, the latter type of information is “cross-referenced with major linguistic information platforms such as _Ethnologue_ (Lewis 2009) and _Glottolog_ (Hammarström et al. 2022)” (NLLB Team et al. 2022: 17). Unlike Glottolog, which is administered by a group of typological linguists associated with western academic institutions such as universities and the Max-Planck Institute, Ethnologue is linked to the _Summer Institute of Linguistic_ (SIL), probably the largest and most active modern Christian missionary organization (see Sect.3). While links to Ethnologue are understood as legitimating the validity and social adequacy of the activities of NLLB, the colonial roots of these practices remain invisible.

## 4 Language making for machine learning technologies
There is also resistance to the continuing domination of communities by capitalist actors from the Global North. Some communities refuse to work with large technology companies or modern missionary organizations such as SIL and develop their own writing systems and language corpora using a grassroots approach to control what is happening to their language. Others either refuse to make their language available for digital processing (e.g., the Maori community, see Hao [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-025-02389-5#ref-CR24 "Hao K (2022) A new vision of artificial intelligence for the people. MIT Technology Review,   
                  https://www.technologyreview.com/2022/04/22/1050394/artificial-intelligence-for-the-people/
.")) or, what seems to become more frequent now, they partner up with university based researchers to develop viable systems (e.g., https://www.masakhane.io/home—note, however, that Google is co-funding the initiative, see https://lacunafund.org/funders/). Grassroots approaches can be effectively deployed in the initial stages that focus on the development of orthographies, word lists, basic grammars and small text collections such as through low-cost collaboration between linguists and interested community members. However, the scaling of such work to integrate a language into machine learning processes is much more complicated as it requires access to considerable funding and computation resources besides computational knowhow. Both are not easily accessible even for members working at educational institutions in the Global North. This means that it is generally difficult and expensive for communities to develop digital and AI technologies without collaborating with big tech.

## 4 Language making for machine learning technologies
The final step before automatic translation starts involves creation of a viable starter training and test data set for training the multilingual model of Flores-200This is referred to as ‘seed data’ and described as “a set of professionally-translated sentences in the Wikipedia domain” (NLLB Team et al. 2022: 23). Due to being human produced and thus less likely to contain hallucinations (Förster and Skop, this volume), it is presented as vital for ensuring high-quality translation outputs. The development of ‘seed data’ follows the same overall procedure as that used to create the ‘benchmark’ data set, see Fig.1, but “consists of translations from 842 distinct web articles, totaling 3001 sentences” (NLLB Team et al. 2022: 22). These sentences are assembled using an intricate process presumably to ensure some elusive notion of representativeness. The process is described as follows:
> Data for NLLB-Seed was sampled from Wikimedia’s _List of articles every Wikipedia should have_, a collection of 10,000 Wikidata IDs corresponding to notable topics in different fields of knowledge and human activity. These are split into 11 categories such as _People, History, Philosophy and Religion, Geography_. We uniformly sampled a subset of IDs from which we would draw data, and mapped these to the corresponding English Wikipedia articles. From each of these articles we then sampled the data that would be sent to translators. Instead of extracting individual sentences, which would have left translators with little context to work with, we chose to sample triplets of contiguous sentences, ensuring no more than one triplet per article was used (similar to Flores-200). (NLLB Team et al. 2022: 23-24).
texts.39:
## 4 Language making for machine learning technologies
The resulting human translations are checked by automatic processes (cf Kreutzer et al. [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-025-02389-5#ref-CR30 "Kreutzer J et al. (2021) Quality at a glance: an audit of web-crawled multilingual datasets. Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics,   
                  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2103.12028.pdf
.")) before they are used for training. Although this process is hailed as groundbreaking (NLLB Team et al. 2022: 23), persistent challenges such as mistranslations and other kinds of hallucinations remain.
The selection of languages for such artificial data creation is presented as a principle-based process. For example, to obtain a list of 200 languages, NLLB Team et al. (2022: 12) initially created “a preliminary list of over 250 possible language candidates”, and then whittled it down to 200 languages as follows:
> First, we considered all languages with a Wikipedia presence. [...] Wikipedia is a key site of knowledge dissemination for many speaking low-resource languages [...]  
>   
>   
> Next, we solicited lists of languages spoken in various regions by native speakers, focusing particularly on African languages—a category of languages that have historically been underrepresented in translation efforts (Nekoto et al., 2020).  
>   
>   
> We then examined language coverage in multiple existing datasets in the natural language processing community, paying focused attention on training datasets without accompanying evaluation datasets.  
>   
>   
> Finally, we considered the adoption and usage of each language by looking at the approximate number of native speakers and other community-level variables relevant to our work.  
>   
>   
> Next, for each of the language candidates, we partnered with linguists from various specialized language service providers to understand if each of these languages has a standardized written form [...] because having a reliable, high-quality evaluation dataset is critical to accelerated experimental progress (NLLB Team et al. 2022: 12, 16).
texts.40:
## 4 Language making for machine learning technologies
This procedure illustrates the ‘opportunity of optimization’ approach that drives commercial entities’ engagement: the selection of languages is guided by easy and cheap access to data and the potential to reap monetary profits rather than the much cited concerns for improving the lives of disenfranchised people. This is also openly admitted when they state that: “deciding which languages to include in the final list ultimately came down to assessing the potential impact we might have on the respective low-resource language communities” (NLLB Team et al. 2022: 17) and “many of the languages that made the final cut have a presence on Wikipedia” (NLLB Team et al. 2022: 17). By contrast, languages with low speaker numbers that lack “written standards or [that] are predominantly oral” (NLLB Team et al. 2022: 17), whose cosmologies do not easily fit with the western symbolic order, or, interestingly, for whom the team could not identify clear needs for machine translation (for unspecified reasons) or sensed potential (undefined) risks were excluded.
texts.41:
## 4 Language making for machine learning technologies
Once identified for inclusion, languages are also categorized for easy digital access further fashioning them into discrete tangible artifacts, and ensuring alignment with existing language regimes in the Global North. NLLB, for instance, classifies each language in Flores-200 by recording its web support such as whether it is supported by Google Translate and Microsoft Translate, its resource level, i.e., “if there are fewer than 1 M publicly available, de-duplicated bitext samples with any other language within our set of 200 languages” (NLLB Team et al. 2022: 17) and by assigning it an ISO 639–3 code, a ISO 15924 script subtag, and a unique name, which is necessary “due to formatting limitations” even though a language might locally be identified by multiple names. Interestingly, the latter type of information is “cross-referenced with major linguistic information platforms such as _Ethnologue_ (Lewis 2009) and _Glottolog_ (Hammarström et al. 2022)” (NLLB Team et al. 2022: 17). Unlike Glottolog, which is administered by a group of typological linguists associated with western academic institutions such as universities and the Max-Planck Institute, Ethnologue is linked to the _Summer Institute of Linguistic_ (SIL), probably the largest and most active modern Christian missionary organization (see Sect.3). While links to Ethnologue are understood as legitimating the validity and social adequacy of the activities of NLLB, the colonial roots of these practices remain invisible.
texts.42:
## 4 Language making for machine learning technologies
There is also resistance to the continuing domination of communities by capitalist actors from the Global North. Some communities refuse to work with large technology companies or modern missionary organizations such as SIL and develop their own writing systems and language corpora using a grassroots approach to control what is happening to their language. Others either refuse to make their language available for digital processing (e.g., the Maori community, see Hao [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-025-02389-5#ref-CR24 "Hao K (2022) A new vision of artificial intelligence for the people. MIT Technology Review,   
                  https://www.technologyreview.com/2022/04/22/1050394/artificial-intelligence-for-the-people/
.")) or, what seems to become more frequent now, they partner up with university based researchers to develop viable systems (e.g., https://www.masakhane.io/home—note, however, that Google is co-funding the initiative, see https://lacunafund.org/funders/). Grassroots approaches can be effectively deployed in the initial stages that focus on the development of orthographies, word lists, basic grammars and small text collections such as through low-cost collaboration between linguists and interested community members. However, the scaling of such work to integrate a language into machine learning processes is much more complicated as it requires access to considerable funding and computation resources besides computational knowhow. Both are not easily accessible even for members working at educational institutions in the Global North. This means that it is generally difficult and expensive for communities to develop digital and AI technologies without collaborating with big tech.

The final step before automatic translation starts involves creation of a viable starter training and test data set for training the multilingual model of Flores-200This is referred to as ‘seed data’ and described as “a set of professionally-translated sentences in the Wikipedia domain” (NLLB Team et al. 2022: 23). Due to being human produced and thus less likely to contain hallucinations (Förster and Skop, this volume), it is presented as vital for ensuring high-quality translation outputs. The development of ‘seed data’ follows the same overall procedure as that used to create the ‘benchmark’ data set, see Fig.1, but “consists of translations from 842 distinct web articles, totaling 3001 sentences” (NLLB Team et al. 2022: 22). These sentences are assembled using an intricate process presumably to ensure some elusive notion of representativeness. The process is described as follows:
> Data for NLLB-Seed was sampled from Wikimedia’s _List of articles every Wikipedia should have_, a collection of 10,000 Wikidata IDs corresponding to notable topics in different fields of knowledge and human activity. These are split into 11 categories such as _People, History, Philosophy and Religion, Geography_. We uniformly sampled a subset of IDs from which we would draw data, and mapped these to the corresponding English Wikipedia articles. From each of these articles we then sampled the data that would be sent to translators. Instead of extracting individual sentences, which would have left translators with little context to work with, we chose to sample triplets of contiguous sentences, ensuring no more than one triplet per article was used (similar to Flores-200). (NLLB Team et al. 2022: 23-24).

## 4 Language making for machine learning technologies
The resulting human translations are checked by automatic processes (cf Kreutzer et al. [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-025-02389-5#ref-CR30 "Kreutzer J et al. (2021) Quality at a glance: an audit of web-crawled multilingual datasets. Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics,   
                  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2103.12028.pdf
.")) before they are used for training. Although this process is hailed as groundbreaking (NLLB Team et al. 2022: 23), persistent challenges such as mistranslations and other kinds of hallucinations remain.
The selection of languages for such artificial data creation is presented as a principle-based process. For example, to obtain a list of 200 languages, NLLB Team et al. (2022: 12) initially created “a preliminary list of over 250 possible language candidates”, and then whittled it down to 200 languages as follows:
> First, we considered all languages with a Wikipedia presence. [...] Wikipedia is a key site of knowledge dissemination for many speaking low-resource languages [...]  
>   
>   
> Next, we solicited lists of languages spoken in various regions by native speakers, focusing particularly on African languages—a category of languages that have historically been underrepresented in translation efforts (Nekoto et al., 2020).  
>   
>   
> We then examined language coverage in multiple existing datasets in the natural language processing community, paying focused attention on training datasets without accompanying evaluation datasets.  
>   
>   
> Finally, we considered the adoption and usage of each language by looking at the approximate number of native speakers and other community-level variables relevant to our work.  
>   
>   
> Next, for each of the language candidates, we partnered with linguists from various specialized language service providers to understand if each of these languages has a standardized written form [...] because having a reliable, high-quality evaluation dataset is critical to accelerated experimental progress (NLLB Team et al. 2022: 12, 16).

## 4 Language making for machine learning technologies
This procedure illustrates the ‘opportunity of optimization’ approach that drives commercial entities’ engagement: the selection of languages is guided by easy and cheap access to data and the potential to reap monetary profits rather than the much cited concerns for improving the lives of disenfranchised people. This is also openly admitted when they state that: “deciding which languages to include in the final list ultimately came down to assessing the potential impact we might have on the respective low-resource language communities” (NLLB Team et al. 2022: 17) and “many of the languages that made the final cut have a presence on Wikipedia” (NLLB Team et al. 2022: 17). By contrast, languages with low speaker numbers that lack “written standards or [that] are predominantly oral” (NLLB Team et al. 2022: 17), whose cosmologies do not easily fit with the western symbolic order, or, interestingly, for whom the team could not identify clear needs for machine translation (for unspecified reasons) or sensed potential (undefined) risks were excluded.

## 4 Language making for machine learning technologies
Once identified for inclusion, languages are also categorized for easy digital access further fashioning them into discrete tangible artifacts, and ensuring alignment with existing language regimes in the Global North. NLLB, for instance, classifies each language in Flores-200 by recording its web support such as whether it is supported by Google Translate and Microsoft Translate, its resource level, i.e., “if there are fewer than 1 M publicly available, de-duplicated bitext samples with any other language within our set of 200 languages” (NLLB Team et al. 2022: 17) and by assigning it an ISO 639–3 code, a ISO 15924 script subtag, and a unique name, which is necessary “due to formatting limitations” even though a language might locally be identified by multiple names. There is also resistance to the continuing domination of communities by capitalist actors from the Global North. Some communities refuse to work with large technology companies or modern missionary organizations such as SIL and develop their own writing systems and language corpora using a grassroots approach to control what is happening to their language. Others either refuse to make their language available for digital processing (e.g., the Maori community, see Hao [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-025-02389-5#ref-CR24 "Hao K (2022) A new vision of artificial intelligence for the people. MIT Technology Review,   
                  https://www.technologyreview.com/2022/04/22/1050394/artificial-intelligence-for-the-people/
.")) or, what seems to become more frequent now, they partner up with university based researchers to develop viable systems (e.g., https://www.masakhane.io/home—note, however, that Google is co-funding the initiative, see https://lacunafund.org/funders/). Both are not easily accessible even for members working at educational institutions in the Global North. This means that it is generally difficult and expensive for communities to develop digital and AI technologies without collaborating with big tech.

Title: Bible Translation - Willamette International
Chunks: 0
Willamette International partnered with SIL Cameroon in Cameroon, Central Africa, in 2020 to help provide administration and management support personnel in the work of Bible Translation and language development. Cameroon has around 280 languages. Between the collaboration of SIL Cameroon and other translation organizations, about 120 of the languages have all or portions of the Bible translated into them. SIL Cameroon is currently working on 25 translation projects.
“SIL Cameroon is affiliated with SIL International, a faith-based nonprofit organization, aimed at serving language communities worldwide. Since 1969, SIL Cameroon has partnered with language communities throughout Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea, building their capacity for sustainable language development by means of research, translation, training and materials development” (https://www.silcam.org/).
The specific support work in which Willamette International missionary staff is currently involved is management of the SIL centers in Yaoundé, the capital of Cameroon. These centers provide long-term housing, guest housing, the head offices for SIL Cameroon and much-needed space for language and translation related training. Training is a major area of focus as it is SIL Cameroon’s desire to pass on the baton of translation from expatriates to Cameroonian nationals. When training is not taking place, the guest housing and meeting rooms are rented out to other mission organizations, churches or faith-based schools to use for retreats, conferences and other events.
It is our desire to meet the practical needs of Bible translation, but most of all to see lives transformed by Jesus Christ through God’s Word and God-given opportunities to share His Word in Cameroon.

This procedure illustrates the ‘opportunity of optimization’ approach that drives commercial entities’ engagement: the selection of languages is guided by easy and cheap access to data and the potential to reap monetary profits rather than the much cited concerns for improving the lives of disenfranchised people. This is also openly admitted when they state that: “deciding which languages to include in the final list ultimately came down to assessing the potential impact we might have on the respective low-resource language communities” (NLLB Team et al. 2022: 17) and “many of the languages that made the final cut have a presence on Wikipedia” (NLLB Team et al. 2022: 17). By contrast, languages with low speaker numbers that lack “written standards or [that] are predominantly oral” (NLLB Team et al. 2022: 17), whose cosmologies do not easily fit with the western symbolic order, or, interestingly, for whom the team could not identify clear needs for machine translation (for unspecified reasons) or sensed potential (undefined) risks were excluded.

## 4 Language making for machine learning technologies
Once identified for inclusion, languages are also categorized for easy digital access further fashioning them into discrete tangible artifacts, and ensuring alignment with existing language regimes in the Global North. NLLB, for instance, classifies each language in Flores-200 by recording its web support such as whether it is supported by Google Translate and Microsoft Translate, its resource level, i.e., “if there are fewer than 1 M publicly available, de-duplicated bitext samples with any other language within our set of 200 languages” (NLLB Team et al. 2022: 17) and by assigning it an ISO 639–3 code, a ISO 15924 script subtag, and a unique name, which is necessary “due to formatting limitations” even though a language might locally be identified by multiple names. Interestingly, the latter type of information is “cross-referenced with major linguistic information platforms such as _Ethnologue_ (Lewis 2009) and _Glottolog_ (Hammarström et al. 2022)” (NLLB Team et al. 2022: 17). Unlike Glottolog, which is administered by a group of typological linguists associated with western academic institutions such as universities and the Max-Planck Institute, Ethnologue is linked to the _Summer Institute of Linguistic_ (SIL), probably the largest and most active modern Christian missionary organization (see Sect.3). While links to Ethnologue are understood as legitimating the validity and social adequacy of the activities of NLLB, the colonial roots of these practices remain invisible.

## 4 Language making for machine learning technologies
There is also resistance to the continuing domination of communities by capitalist actors from the Global North. Some communities refuse to work with large technology companies or modern missionary organizations such as SIL and develop their own writing systems and language corpora using a grassroots approach to control what is happening to their language. Others either refuse to make their language available for digital processing (e.g., the Maori community, see Hao [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-025-02389-5#ref-CR24 "Hao K (2022) A new vision of artificial intelligence for the people. MIT Technology Review,   
                  https://www.technologyreview.com/2022/04/22/1050394/artificial-intelligence-for-the-people/
.")) or, what seems to become more frequent now, they partner up with university based researchers to develop viable systems (e.g., https://www.masakhane.io/home—note, however, that Google is co-funding the initiative, see https://lacunafund.org/funders/). Grassroots approaches can be effectively deployed in the initial stages that focus on the development of orthographies, word lists, basic grammars and small text collections such as through low-cost collaboration between linguists and interested community members. However, the scaling of such work to integrate a language into machine learning processes is much more complicated as it requires access to considerable funding and computation resources besides computational knowhow. Both are not easily accessible even for members working at educational institutions in the Global North. This means that it is generally difficult and expensive for communities to develop digital and AI technologies without collaborating with big tech.

Willamette International partnered with SIL Cameroon in Cameroon, Central Africa, in 2020 to help provide administration and management support personnel in the work of Bible Translation and language development. Cameroon has around 280 languages. Between the collaboration of SIL Cameroon and other translation organizations, about 120 of the languages have all or portions of the Bible translated into them. SIL Cameroon is currently working on 25 translation projects.
“SIL Cameroon is affiliated with SIL International, a faith-based nonprofit organization, aimed at serving language communities worldwide. Since 1969, SIL Cameroon has partnered with language communities throughout Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea, building their capacity for sustainable language development by means of research, translation, training and materials development” (https://www.silcam.org/).
The specific support work in which Willamette International missionary staff is currently involved is management of the SIL centers in Yaoundé, the capital of Cameroon. These centers provide long-term housing, guest housing, the head offices for SIL Cameroon and much-needed space for language and translation related training. Training is a major area of focus as it is SIL Cameroon’s desire to pass on the baton of translation from expatriates to Cameroonian nationals. When training is not taking place, the guest housing and meeting rooms are rented out to other mission organizations, churches or faith-based schools to use for retreats, conferences and other events.
It is our desire to meet the practical needs of Bible translation, but most of all to see lives transformed by Jesus Christ through God’s Word and God-given opportunities to share His Word in Cameroon.

## 3 The colonial making of language: from missionaries to ISO codes
"): 71) and is closely connected to _Wycliffe Bible Translators_, whose expressed aim is to disseminate the Bible through translation to as many language communities as possible. SIL has trained and supported over 5000 missionary linguists who have engaged in the study of more than 1000 languages around the world, mostly in the Global South (Errington 2008). Their missionary linguists are financed by their congregations in the Global North, particularly in North America. On the one hand, SIL missionaries ‘facilitate’ bible translations and related ‘language development’ work by making tools, expertise, and people available to create written codes out of local oral language practices, to develop written and digital artifacts and literacy materials based on them; they also facilitate literacy campaigns based on the developed materials. On the other hand, through the organization’s coordination, editing, and publishing of _Ethnologue_, “the single largest, most widely cited compendium of knowledge of global linguistic diversity” (Errington 153), they are taking a lead in geographically mapping, defining, differentiating languages worldwide; in short systematizing and standardizing linguistic diversity worldwide.
Since 1976, the “hallmark of the _Ethnologue_ has been the three letter code” (Kamusella [2012](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-025-02389-5#ref-CR28 "Kamusella T (2012) The global regime of language recognition. Int J Sociol Lang 218:59–86.   
                  https://doi.org/10.1515/ijsl-2012-0059
texts.28:
## 3 The colonial making of language: from missionaries to ISO codes
"): 72) which, like an international airport code, functions to uniquely identify languages across political boundaries “where the same language may be called by different names, and in distinguishing different languages called by the same name” (History of the Ethnologue [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-025-02389-5#ref-CR26 "History of the Ethnologue (2024)   
                  https://www.ethnologue.com/history/  
                    
                . Accessed 27 May 2024")). In 2002, the world’s main organization for developing and administering industrial standards, the _International Organization for Standardization_ charged SIL with developing a three letter ISO code (Code 639) for classifying all the languages of the world. Since 2007, SIL has been functioning as the registration institution for all languages.
> This code allocation is the actual uniformized worldwide registration of languages that amounts to their de facto international recognition. It also appears to be de jure (though not overtly articulated as such) recognition in light of international law, insofar as the International Organization for Standardization creates and maintains elements and procedures of this law. [...]. But this code allocation does have the effect of providing a form of administrative assertion by a duly authorized body on behalf of the global community that a language is a language, not a dialect. (Kamusella [2012](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-025-02389-5#ref-CR28 "Kamusella T (2012) The global regime of language recognition. Int J Sociol Lang 218:59–86.   
>                   https://doi.org/10.1515/ijsl-2012-0059  
>                     
>                 "): 72)

## 3 The colonial making of language: from missionaries to ISO codes
Ideally, speakers should register languages. However, in practice many speaker communities lack access to and interest in this enumerative standardizing process and thus registration is effectively usually initiated by corporate, state, and religious institutions from the Global North that have a vested interest in systematizing, categorizing, enumerating, and ordering linguistic practices for their own commercial, political, and religious purposes. Via SIL, the Ethnologue and the tradition of ISO codes, there is a direct continuation of colonial language traditions in computational culture: ISO codes are implemented whenever a language enters the domain of computing. Today, this function of ISO-code 639 is central, as described on the website of the organization:
> ISO 639, Code for individual languages and language groups, can be applied across many types of organization and situations. It is needed for the basic settings of billions of user interfaces to ICT systems and devices, as well as for the indication of different language versions of websites. It is indispensable for information management in publishing, librarianship, and for large networks
https://www.iso.org/iso-639-language-code (Date of Access: 27.5.2024).
We discuss other forms of continuation but also the reconfiguration of colonial language making in contexts of computing and AI in the next section.
texts.30:
## 4 Language making for machine learning technologies
The making of languages in digital technologies, like the missionary linguistics tradition, is based on the assumption that languages are objects in the world and that data sets represent or even _are_ languages. If a language is used for computation practices, it is referred to with an ISO code. Unlike missionary times where engagement with speakers was crucial for the creation of a language and its artifacts, in the digital industry, data sets, if available, are mostly taken in digital formats from the web (Schneider [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-025-02389-5#ref-CR54 "Schneider B (2022) Multilingualism and AI – the regimentation of language in the age of digital capitalism. Signs Soc.   
                  https://doi.org/10.1086/721757
")). Practices of transforming interactional practice into data (digital data in this case) and translation also remain central in processes in the age of machine learning. Besides digital corpus curation and construction, translation is centrally used in developing data standards for languages and training data for machine learning. Translated or parallel texts are employed to make language technology algorithms work, which we discuss in more detail below. Digital technology companies cast data creation and translation, and particularly their automatic production, as a sort of charitable work that will make an important contribution to changing the world’s current social status quo (Bommasani et al. [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-025-02389-5#ref-CR5 "Bommasani R et al (2021) On the opportunities and risks of foundation models. Center for Research on Foundation Models (CRFM) – Stanford University,   
                  https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.07258  
                    
                ")).
texts.31:
## 4 Language making for machine learning technologies
To illustrate how language data are produced and subsequently used to construct language technologies, we focus on one specific publication. This is the text _No Language Left Behind_ (NLLB Team et al. 2022), which has been published by Meta, UC Berkeley and John Hopkins University. It introduces a technological method—referred to as ‘Flores 200’—to develop machine translation for under-resourced languages. At the time of writing this text, Big Tech companies invest a lot of resources in the creation of language technologies for minority languages, the majority of which are non-European and non-standardized languages. This has to be understood against the background of surveillance capitalism and data colonialism (see above). There are also other such projects (see e.g., Siddhant et al [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-025-02389-5#ref-CR56 "Siddhant A et al (2022) Building machine translation systems for the next thousand languages. arXiv   
                  https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.03983
."), a Google project) but we here focus on the _No Language Left Behind_ publication as it gives detailed access into how minority language data is generated and used. As can be inferred from its title, which closely resembles the name of a US education bill championed by the George W. Bush administration (_No Child Left Behind_) that was designed to enhance minority and poor children’s educational outcomes, the publication reproduces the colonial endeavor of making languages fit for (Western) language and technology practices couching it in colonial discursive tropes of ‘caring about’ and ‘helping’ the ‘Other’ (Mejias and Couldry 2024 call this 'Data's new civilising mission', Ch.3).Footnote 2
texts.38:
## 4 Language making for machine learning technologies
The final step before automatic translation starts involves creation of a viable starter training and test data set for training the multilingual model of Flores-200This is referred to as ‘seed data’ and described as “a set of professionally-translated sentences in the Wikipedia domain” (NLLB Team et al. 2022: 23). Due to being human produced and thus less likely to contain hallucinations (Förster and Skop, this volume), it is presented as vital for ensuring high-quality translation outputs. The development of ‘seed data’ follows the same overall procedure as that used to create the ‘benchmark’ data set, see Fig.1, but “consists of translations from 842 distinct web articles, totaling 3001 sentences” (NLLB Team et al. 2022: 22). These sentences are assembled using an intricate process presumably to ensure some elusive notion of representativeness. The process is described as follows:
> Data for NLLB-Seed was sampled from Wikimedia’s _List of articles every Wikipedia should have_, a collection of 10,000 Wikidata IDs corresponding to notable topics in different fields of knowledge and human activity. These are split into 11 categories such as _People, History, Philosophy and Religion, Geography_. We uniformly sampled a subset of IDs from which we would draw data, and mapped these to the corresponding English Wikipedia articles. From each of these articles we then sampled the data that would be sent to translators. Instead of extracting individual sentences, which would have left translators with little context to work with, we chose to sample triplets of contiguous sentences, ensuring no more than one triplet per article was used (similar to Flores-200). (NLLB Team et al. 2022: 23-24).
texts.39:
## 4 Language making for machine learning technologies
The resulting human translations are checked by automatic processes (cf Kreutzer et al. [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-025-02389-5#ref-CR30 "Kreutzer J et al. (2021) Quality at a glance: an audit of web-crawled multilingual datasets. Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics,   
                  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2103.12028.pdf
.")) before they are used for training. Although this process is hailed as groundbreaking (NLLB Team et al. 2022: 23), persistent challenges such as mistranslations and other kinds of hallucinations remain.
The selection of languages for such artificial data creation is presented as a principle-based process. For example, to obtain a list of 200 languages, NLLB Team et al. (2022: 12) initially created “a preliminary list of over 250 possible language candidates”, and then whittled it down to 200 languages as follows:
> First, we considered all languages with a Wikipedia presence. [...] Wikipedia is a key site of knowledge dissemination for many speaking low-resource languages [...]  
>   
>   
> Next, we solicited lists of languages spoken in various regions by native speakers, focusing particularly on African languages—a category of languages that have historically been underrepresented in translation efforts (Nekoto et al., 2020).  
>   
>   
> We then examined language coverage in multiple existing datasets in the natural language processing community, paying focused attention on training datasets without accompanying evaluation datasets.  
>   
>   
> Finally, we considered the adoption and usage of each language by looking at the approximate number of native speakers and other community-level variables relevant to our work.  
>   
>   
> Next, for each of the language candidates, we partnered with linguists from various specialized language service providers to understand if each of these languages has a standardized written form [...] because having a reliable, high-quality evaluation dataset is critical to accelerated experimental progress (NLLB Team et al. 2022: 12, 16).
